I’m running into the following problem: I am following the current advice of using 2x the last base fee for the max fee and hard coding 1 gwei for the priority fee, but… The current base fee on Calaveras is 7 **wei**. So 14 wei, is far less than the 1 gwei being hard-coded for the priority, which is failing. So, what is a better way to estimate values. 🙂 Should the maxfee always be the min(2*baseFee, 2 * baseFee + priorityFee) This needs a “good” solution; I feel like some will say “on the real network it will never be 7wei”, but we need to keep in mind there will be testnets and ilk where this can still be true. Base fee is atrociously tiny. Compared to 1 gwei default priority. Priority fee != base fee. I know. My recommendation for launch is `2 * baseFeePerGas + priorityFeePerGas`. That means on networks with a low baseFee, the priority fee is 100’s of millions times more expensive than the base fee. And for launch I recommend `priorityFeePerGas = 2e9`, though with the new JSON-RPC endpoint being worked on you could do a tad better. This is expected and correct. The priority fee is expected to dwarf the base fee? Priority fee is to offset uncle risk, which is a function of block propagation time and block reward. The two are not related to each other. In some cases, one will dwarf the other, in others it will be the other way around. One should not assume that base fee is always on the same order of magnitude as the priority fee. That is, they move completely independent of each other and they are not a function of the same inputs. I agree. But the hard-coded value is making even less sense on unpopular networks. We def need a better way to approximate it. On Ropsten, a priority fee of ~1e9 is still very much correct. maxFee = 1000000014 and priority fee = 1000000000 seems weird. :p On Rinkeby/Goerli things get *way* more complicated since they are proof of authority so uncle risk calculations are incredibly different. I don't know if anyone has calculated it. But ok. I’ll make that the built in defaults. Why does it seem weird? That would be like ordering a $3 soda from a restaurant and paying $500 million as a tip. There are *many* restaurants where the cost of the food is dwarfed by the cost of the service. 🙂 It is just that in most cases they don't bill separately for the two. Also, on a PoA network, uncle risk is negligible. 🙂 Yeah, on PoA things are different but I don't think anyone has taken the time to calculate a "correct" priority fee. Also, since they are just test networks I don't think anyone actually cares. 🤷 True. /) 🙂 A $100 steak is like $5 in meat, $5 in cooking, $90 in "fancy wait staff and ambiance". Yes, but I’d only leave $20 tip. 🙂 I don't think you should compare US tips, because they do not make economic sense. Service costs should be considered rolled into the baseFee. We are trying to build an economically rational system here, not mirror an economically irrational system. 😄 The baseFee is the cost of doing business + necessary profit to remain operating. (another reason I despise the term `tip` for priority fee, it makes people think about the problem wrong) 😉 Anyways. That’s why it seems weird. But it’s easy to do. Base fee is not the cost of doing business. Base fee is the market rate for blockspace. Priority fee is closer to the "cost of doing business". Given a limited resource and more demand for that resource than supply, the price goes up until supply == demand (as demand exits due to price being too high). This is totally unrelated to operational costs, this is just a mechanism to figure out "who wants in more". Priority fee is essentially operational cost of miners (ish). Also, can you point me to maths for computing a given block’s baseFee? Right now I’m using 2x getBlock(-1).baseFee, but it should probably be something more math-sound based on block(-1) baseFee and gasUsed/gasTarget (also, I didn’t see a gasTarget on the block). ```python if INITIAL_FORK_BLOCK_NUMBER == block.number: expected_base_fee_per_gas = INITIAL_BASE_FEE elif parent_gas_used == parent_gas_target: expected_base_fee_per_gas = parent_base_fee_per_gas elif parent_gas_used > parent_gas_target: gas_used_delta = parent_gas_used - parent_gas_target base_fee_per_gas_delta = max(parent_base_fee_per_gas * gas_used_delta // parent_gas_target // BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR, 1) expected_base_fee_per_gas = parent_base_fee_per_gas + base_fee_per_gas_delta else: gas_used_delta = parent_gas_target - parent_gas_used base_fee_per_gas_delta = parent_base_fee_per_gas * gas_used_delta // parent_gas_target // BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR expected_base_fee_per_gas = max(parent_base_fee_per_gas - base_fee_per_gas_delta, 0) assert expected_base_fee_per_gas == block.base_fee_per_gas, 'invalid block: base fee not correct' ``` (from EIP-1559) For `parent_*` you would use the `latest` block details, and the `expected_base_fee_per_gas` will be the base fee of the next block. Pragmatically, I think `2 * eth_getBlockByNumber('latest').baseFeePerGas` is very reasonable. That `2` in there is pretty arbitrary and in most cases dwarfs the difference between `latest.baseFeePerGas` and `pending.baseFeePerGas`. `gasTarget = block.gasLimit / 2` basefee seems more like a deflation tax than a market rate for blockspace :> because first of all it gets burned and second of all its determined by an algorithm. So its more of a tax than a market rate. Just my humble opinion. And it has a minimum of 7? Or is that guaranteed by the maths? Just a side effect of the maths. I recommend testing < 7 cases if you want to be thorough (like make sure it can walk up from 0) if you are implementing stuff. Perfect. Specifically, the 7 minimum is a side effect of integer math rounding and can change if some of the constants change (like the rate of change). Which is why I recommend against hard coding a minimum, because then you'll have a bug if that constant changes in a future hard fork. Yeah. If integer rounding works, I prefer that. If it doesn't, it means you round differently than the rest of the clients. 😄 (round up vs round down) Lol! I assume truncation. 🙂 "Round toward 0", which I think is synonymous with truncation? But for now I may just stick with the 2x baseFee. But I’ll add a comment about this. Yeah. We specifically avoided negative numbers in the algorithm because apparently rounding negatives differs a lot across languages. Rounding down vs. rounding towards 0. 🙂 (round toward 0 vs round toward negative infinity) Exactly. That was something I didn't know was highly debated in math circles until this project. 😬 Apparently, both have arguments for why they are "right". Also the correct usage of underflow. Which is unrelated to overflow. Maybe a silly question, but how do we calculate the exact cost of a transaction? Scenario, I want to transfer all the Ether from one account to another, without leaving crumbs. I know the base fee for the latest block is x, and I want to pay a service fee to the miners of y. But we apply the 2x baseFee.. There is a big chance that a portion of the amount will be returned Sweeping is hard. You can force a sweep by setting maxFee and maxPriorityFee to the same value, but this basically just burns any excess money. Useful if you care about actually clearing the value from the account, not useful for maximizing the amount out. I would support someone creating an EIP for a new "sweep" transaction type specifically for dealing with this situation. Yep, i thought of that, but if maxFee and maxPriorityFee are the same, how are we accounting for the baseFee? Edit: Ok I got it.. base fee will be discounted anyway from the miners fee. It isn't great, but if the person wants their account to "go to zero" that is the way to do it. It basically says, "pay this much fee, give any leftovers to the miner". did we get this info? excerpts.author: ricmoo
excerpts.content: Also, can you point me to maths for computing a given block’s baseFee? Right now I’m using 2x getBlock(-1).baseFee, but it should probably be something more math-sound based on block(-1) baseFee and gasUsed/gasTarget (also, I didn’t see a gasTarget on the block).

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
```python
if INITIAL_FORK_BLOCK_NUMBER == block.number:
    expected_base_fee_per_gas = INITIAL_BASE_FEE
elif parent_gas_used == parent_gas_target:
    expected_base_fee_per_gas = parent_base_fee_per_gas
elif parent_gas_used > parent_gas_target:
    gas_used_delta = parent_gas_used - parent_gas_target
    base_fee_per_gas_delta = max(parent_base_fee_per_gas * gas_used_delta // parent_gas_target // BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR, 1)
    expected_base_fee_per_gas = parent_base_fee_per_gas + base_fee_per_gas_delta
else:
    gas_used_delta = parent_gas_target - parent_gas_used
    base_fee_per_gas_delta = parent_base_fee_per_gas * gas_used_delta // parent_gas_target // BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR
    expected_base_fee_per_gas = max(parent_base_fee_per_gas - base_fee_per_gas_delta, 0)
assert expected_base_fee_per_gas == block.base_fee_per_gas, 'invalid block: base fee not correct'
```
